newsitem.title: Albania: Investors launch new protest in southern Albania.
newsitem.headline: Investors launch new protest in southern Albania.

text.p: Thousands of Albanians facing ruin from collapsed investment schemes fought street battles with police on Wednesday and eventually persuaded them to allow their anti-government protest to proceed.
Equipped with water cannon and dogs and firing in the air, police tried twice to disperse up to 7,000 protesters demanding refunds and chanting slogans against President Sali Berisha.
The clashes were the first since widespread rioting last month in protest against the shady funds in Europe's poorest country, prompting mass arrests on public order charges.
The interior ministry accused "terrorist elements" of injuring three policemen in the initial clashes. It said three protesters were slightly hurt.

As night fell, police moved against marchers for the second time on a tree-lined boulevard. Each side hurled stones and shots rang out. Caught up in the melee were children wearing yellow armbands and dozens of people on crutches.
Officers in the 300-strong cordon gradually heeded appeals by protesters to take off their shields and helmets.

Some handed out cigarettes. "Peace, peace, the police are with us," the crowd chanted. Bonfires of tyres and palm leaves burned through the evening as police backed off and many demonstrators returned home.
"We have nowhere to go, there's no police station here, we're tired and hungry," one policeman said.
The protest was sparked by the collapse on Tuesday of the Gjallica investment scheme, hugely popular in southern Albania.
The Albanian capital Tirana and other cities were quiet, though police were out in force.

Depositors in several cities were receiving refunds of between 50 and 60 percent of their deposits in two other unsuccessful schemes. Distribution was chaotic, with many investors left off lists or holding out for their entire stake.
The demonstration in Vlore was initially dispersed in the morning outside a concert hall but the crowd soon regrouped.
"Berisha is a thief. We'll hang you!" some marchers shouted. "Resign, resign!" others chanted.
Newspapers reported that $350 million to $500 million was tied up in the Gjallica fund. Locals believe as much as $2 billion has been invested in the various pyramids.
Berisha has pledged to help the worst-hit investors, such as those who sold homes to put money into the schemes.
"We are going to open an investigation," he told the Paris daily Le Figaro. "I cannot say (the money) is in Albania."

T he head of the International Monetary Fund, Michel Camdessus, told France's RFI radio the collapse of pyramid schemes would "cost the country dearly, but this is not the end of Albania's transition to a market economy".
Demonstrators set fire last month to government buildings throughout the country. At least 150 people were arrested and prosecutors have threatened long prison terms.

The official ATA news agency reported seven new arrests in the central town of Gramsh. Tirana newspapers said four more people had committed suicide in despair at their lost savings, bringing the number of suicides over the crisis to six.

Berisha's Democratic Party retained power last May in elections denounced by observers as fraudulent. He rejects charges that his government failed to warn investors about the pitfalls of pyramid programmes.
